driver: Data-centre backlash, permitting risk and hyperscaler pullback
trigger_label: Vertiv down more than 10% on the week
second: Local ballot defeats and a Texas governor who backs a moratorium put interconnection and permitting timelines for planned US campuses at risk.
Microsoft is winding down its Oracle lease, cutting neocloud usage and tightening oversight of partner builds, which pushes schedule risk back onto developers.
Power-equipment names (VRT -21%, ETN -7.6% on the week) are de-rated as the market prices slower order growth.
third: Capacity that is already energised and permitted gains scarcity value over greenfield pipelines.
Paying for your own power and offering community benefits becomes the cost of entry, which lifts capex per MW.
Canada, the Nordics and Australia become relative winners for new capacity, though local opposition is spreading there too.
suggest: Lead investor messaging with energised MW, contracted counterparties and the fact that the Texas delay comes from a Microsoft design change, not IREN's execution.
Stress-test the Texas build and the $15bn capex plan against a 6 to 12 month permitting or moratorium delay.
Show customer diversification beyond any single hyperscaler.

driver: AI semis rout and capex-peak debate
trigger_label: SOXX down more than 15% over the month
second: Equity holders are questioning hyperscaler capex near $1tn a year, and the selloff has spread from chips to software (IGV -9.8% over the month).
Asian chip exporters (Samsung, SK Hynix, TSMC, Advantest) carry the second leg, which hits KOSPI and Nikkei liquidity.
GPU resale and recontracting prices become the test of asset value; IREN says it recontracted H100s at double the original price.
third: If capex guidance is cut, GPU-backed ABS and leasing structures face lower collateral values and higher advance-rate haircuts.
Lower equity valuations make converts and ATM programmes more dilutive, which pushes issuers toward secured or project-level debt.
Consolidation favours scaled operators, a point Breakingviews made when it wrote that global muscle will sift out puny data-centre providers.
suggest: Bring recontracting and utilisation data into investor materials to answer the obsolescence question directly.
Model convert and ATM capacity at 20 to 30% lower equity values before planning the next raise.
Track hyperscaler capex commentary into year-end.

driver: Neocloud credit repricing and bank retreat from data-centre loans
second: CoreWeave's 2032 bonds yield above 16%, which resets the yield investors demand for the whole neocloud HY cohort.
ING is auctioning $500m of data-centre loans that include a slice of Stargate, a sign that banks are cutting exposure.
KBRA reports the largest quarterly jump in private-credit defaults, and lenders are tightening terms.
third: Private credit and infrastructure funds that still have capital to deploy gain pricing power, so covenants, cash sweeps and step-ups get stricter.
Investment-grade hyperscaler paper (Meta's bond sale) crowds out lower-rated issuers in the same market.
Contracted take-or-pay revenue with investment-grade counterparties becomes the main way to separate credits.
suggest: Prepare a deal so it can launch fast if the VIX falls back below 20, rather than issuing into the current spread spike.
Compare secured project financing against unsecured high-yield or converts at today's neocloud spreads.
Stress-test liquidity runway if markets stay shut for 3 to 6 months.

driver: Sticky US yields and a hiking Fed
second: The Fed hiked this week and signalled more, and payrolls of 165,000 keep that path open.
Higher base rates raise all-in coupons for data-centre project debt and lower the present value of long-dated leases.
A Democratic Congress limits fiscal expansion but blocks Trump's pressure on the Fed, so rates are less likely to be cut for political reasons.
third: Long-duration infrastructure equity and data-centre REITs (DLR, EQIX) are revalued on cap rates.
Floating-rate private credit stays attractive to lenders but squeezes borrower coverage ratios.
If Tuesday's CPI is hot and the 10-year moves above 5%, a risk-off move could close primary markets for weeks.
suggest: Look at hedging floating-rate exposure or fixing rates on new facilities while the 10-year is below 5%.
Set financing timing around Tuesday's CPI.
Stress-test project returns at a 5.25% 10-year.

driver: Iran war: Hormuz closure versus deal hopes
second: The strait is still closed and tankers keep hitting mines, so prices can jump on any break in Qatar's mediation.
Oil 60% higher year to date keeps headline inflation and central-bank hiking (Fed, RBA, BoE, BoJ) in play.
Gas and LNG markets are tight in Asia and Europe, which raises the marginal cost of power in import-dependent grids.
third: High energy costs sharpen political scrutiny of data-centre power use and electricity bills.
Behind-the-meter gas and fuel cells win share as reliability becomes the priority.
A durable deal would pull headline inflation down quickly and could reopen rate-cut expectations in 2027.
suggest: Present power procurement as fixed or contracted, with little exposure to spot gas spikes.
Run an energy-cost sensitivity at Brent $110 and $80.
Note that renewable and hydro supply at Canadian and Texas sites shields IREN from imported energy prices.

driver: KOSPI crash and Korean chip contagion
trigger_label: KOSPI down more than 8% on the week
second: Circuit breakers, margin calls and leveraged-ETF losses force Korean retail and foreign investors to sell.
The government is waiving collateral rules and weighing a stabilisation fund, so policy is now supporting the market.
Korean retail money is shifting into US stocks and leveraged semis ETFs, which adds to volatility in US AI names.
third: Memory price expectations could soften if hyperscaler orders slow, which would change GPU server cost curves.
A weaker won makes Korean memory exports cheaper and supports Korea's external accounts.
Asian investor appetite for AI-infrastructure paper weakens for now.
suggest: Track HBM supply and pricing as an input to server capex assumptions.
Keep Asian roadshow plans flexible until the KOSPI stabilises.

driver: Nikkei bear market and the BoJ hiking path
trigger_label: Nikkei down more than 15% over the month
second: SoftBank, Advantest and Tokyo Electron are where Japan is most exposed to the AI unwind.
The BoJ, with odds of a December hike near 68%, plus a plan to sell its ETF holdings, means domestic liquidity is tightening.
USD/JPY near 160 raises the risk of intervention and a sharp yen move.
third: A carry-trade unwind would spread volatility across global risk assets and credit.
SoftBank's capacity to fund OpenAI and Stargate commitments comes under scrutiny.
A stronger yen would weigh on Japanese demand for US credit.
suggest: Watch SoftBank and Stargate funding headlines as a signal of the wider AI capex appetite.
Set triggers for risk-off moves around a BoJ December hike.

second: Dovish guidance after the hike, and a weaker AUD, reflect pressure on growth and a recession-like squeeze.
A weaker AUD lifts the AUD value of USD revenue and USD-denominated assets for Australian-listed holders.
Labor is pitching Australia as a destination for data centres while local opposition grows.
third: Australian super funds may increase offshore infrastructure allocations if domestic growth slows.
Federal data-centre policy (power, water, planning) becomes a 2027 political issue.
Spending cuts could slow grid-investment support.
suggest: Present AUD-based investors with USD exposure as a natural hedge.
Engage with Australian policy discussions on data-centre siting and power.

driver: Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi and Xi-Trump-Putin diplomacy
trigger_label: Always on while talks are active
second: A deal framework would weaken the energy risk premium in Europe and ease pressure on gas.
Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure show how much leverage both sides still hold ahead of the talks.
A Xi-Trump-Putin meeting could reshape trade and tariff expectations, including rules on chip exports.
third: Any sanctions relief would change commodity flows, from LNG and oil to uranium enrichment supply.
Gold at $4,075 shows hedging demand will persist until trust improves.
A US security framework for Europe could shift European defence and grid spending.
suggest: Track tariff and chip-export headlines from the Xi-Trump-Putin meeting for supply-chain effects on GPU procurement.
Avoid assuming energy relief in base-case planning.
